claim: Angioblasts that form the major axial blood vessels of the dorsal aorta and cardinal vein migrate toward the embryonic midline from distant lateral positions.
source: Angioblasts that form the major axial blood vessels of the dorsal aorta and cardinal vein migrate toward the embryonic midline from distant lateral positions.
evidence: This is a well-established observation in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Midline angioblast migration requires neighboring tissue rearrangements generated by somite morphogenesis.
source: Using zebrafish, we found that midline angioblast migration requires neighboring tissue rearrangements generated by somite morphogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in multiple figures.

claim: Somitic shape changes cause the adjacent notochord to separate from the underlying endoderm, creating a ventral midline cavity.
source: The somitic shape changes cause the adjacent notochord to separate from the underlying endoderm, creating a ventral midline cavity that provides a physical space for the angioblasts to migrate into.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing the formation of the ventral midline cavity in relation to somite maturation.

claim: The ventral midline cavity provides a physical space for angioblasts to migrate into.
source: The somitic shape changes cause the adjacent notochord to separate from the underlying endoderm, creating a ventral midline cavity that provides a physical space for the angioblasts to migrate into.
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging and sectioning experiments showing angioblasts migrating into the cavity.

claim: The anterior to posterior progression of midline angioblast migration is facilitated by retinoic acid-induced anterior to posterior somite maturation.
source: The anterior to posterior progression of midline angioblast migration is facilitated by retinoic acid-induced anterior to posterior somite maturation and the subsequent progressive opening of the ventral midline cavity.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that RA manipulation affects both somite maturation and angioblast migration timing.

claim: Somite morphogenesis organizes surrounding tissues to facilitate notochord positioning and angioblast migration.
source: Our work demonstrates a critical role for somite morphogenesis in organizing surrounding tissues to facilitate notochord positioning and angioblast migration, which is ultimately responsible for creating a functional cardiovascular system.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Wild-type angioblasts migrate to the midline in a manner consistent with previously described research.
source: Wild-type angioblasts migrated to the midline in a manner consistent with previously described research (Figure 1A, Video 1; Helker et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2005; Kohli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data and citations to previous studies.

claim: aldh1a2 mutants show defects in angioblast migration to the midline.
source: Time-lapse imaging of these embryos shows defects in angioblast migration to the midline (Figure 1B, Video 2), which was also confirmed by in situ hybridization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging and in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: DEAB treatment causes angioblast midline migration defects.
source: Loss of RA by treatment with N,N-diethylaminobenzaldehyde (DEAB) (an inhibitor of the Aldh family, including Aldh1a2; Morgan et al., 2015), the small-molecule retinoic acid receptor (RAR) alpha and gamma inhibitor (BMS453), or expression of a dominant negative RARa using the Tg(hsp70l:eGFP-dnHsa.RARA) transgenic line (hereafter referred to as HS:dnRAR) all caused midline migration defects (Brilli Skvarca et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by multiple methods of RA inhibition all showing similar phenotypes.

claim: BMS453 treatment causes angioblast midline migration defects.
source: Loss of RA by treatment with N,N-diethylaminobenzaldehyde (DEAB) (an inhibitor of the Aldh family, including Aldh1a2; Morgan et al., 2015), the small-molecule retinoic acid receptor (RAR) alpha and gamma inhibitor (BMS453), or expression of a dominant negative RARa using the Tg(hsp70l:eGFP-dnHsa.RARA) transgenic line (hereafter referred to as HS:dnRAR) all caused midline migration defects (Brilli Skvarca et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments.

claim: Expression of dominant negative RARa causes angioblast midline migration defects.
source: Loss of RA by treatment with N,N-diethylaminobenzaldehyde (DEAB) (an inhibitor of the Aldh family, including Aldh1a2; Morgan et al., 2015), the small-molecule retinoic acid receptor (RAR) alpha and gamma inhibitor (BMS453), or expression of a dominant negative RARa using the Tg(hsp70l:eGFP-dnHsa.RARA) transgenic line (hereafter referred to as HS:dnRAR) all caused midline migration defects (Brilli Skvarca et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by genetic manipulation experiments using a transgenic line.

claim: Angioblasts in RA-depleted embryos show delayed migration with disorganized anterior to posterior processivity.
source: Angioblasts in these embryos show delayed migration with disorganized anterior to posterior processivity.
evidence: This is observed in time-lapse imaging of RA-depleted embryos.

claim: Angioblasts treated with RA prematurely initiate migration and arrive earlier to the midline during development.
source: Angioblasts in the DMSO-treated embryos migrate normally, but the angioblasts treated with RA had prematurely initiated migration and arrived earlier to the midline during development (Figure 1C and D, respectively, Video 3).
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging comparing RA-treated and control embryos.

claim: aldh1a2-/- embryos show very low percentage fluorescence at the midline relative to total fluorescence compared to wild-type embryos 4 hr after observation.
source: The aldh1a2-/- embryos show very low percentage fluorescence at the midline, relative to total fluorescence, compared to wild-type embryos 4 hr after observation, when angioblast migration is largely complete (Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is quantified from fluorescence measurements in time-lapse experiments.

claim: Fluorescence is higher at the midline in embryos treated with RA than in DMSO-treated control embryos.
source: On the other hand, fluorescence was higher at the midline in embryos treated with RA than in DMSO-treated control embryos (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is quantified from fluorescence measurements comparing RA-treated and control embryos.

claim: RA is necessary and sufficient for promoting angioblast migration to the midline.
source: This shows that RA is necessary and sufficient for promoting angioblast migration to the midline.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Inhibition of RA at tailbud stage causes angioblast migration defects.
source: Inhibition of RA at tailbud stage caused the angioblast migration defect, but treatment at the five-somite stage resulted in normal migration (Figure 1H and I, respectively), thus establishing the critical developmental window for RA signaling regulation of midline angioblast migration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by stage-specific DEAB treatment experiments.

claim: Treatment with DEAB at the five-somite stage results in normal angioblast migration.
source: Inhibition of RA at tailbud stage caused the angioblast migration defect, but treatment at the five-somite stage resulted in normal migration (Figure 1H and I, respectively), thus establishing the critical developmental window for RA signaling regulation of midline angioblast migration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by stage-specific DEAB treatment experiments.

claim: The critical developmental window for RA signaling regulation of midline angioblast migration is at the tailbud stage.
source: Inhibition of RA at tailbud stage caused the angioblast migration defect, but treatment at the five-somite stage resulted in normal migration (Figure 1H and I, respectively), thus establishing the critical developmental window for RA signaling regulation of midline angioblast migration.
evidence: This is determined by comparing the effects of DEAB treatment at different developmental stages.

claim: Transplanted cells from HS:id3, HS:dnRAR donors exhibit normal migration to the midline in wild-type host embryos.
source: Cells positive for both transgenic constructs were transplanted into tg(kdrl:eGFP) host embryos, and these cells exhibited normal migration to the midline (Figure 2A, Video 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cell transplantation experiments.

claim: The adaxial region of the somites is exposed to RA signaling.
source: The GFP expression indicates tissues that have been exposed to RA. These tissues included the adaxial region of the somites, the notochord, and epidermis (Figure 2B, white arrow, white arrowhead, and gold arrow, respectively).
evidence: This is shown using an RA reporter line with immunohistochemistry.

claim: The notochord is exposed to RA signaling.
source: The GFP expression indicates tissues that have been exposed to RA. These tissues included the adaxial region of the somites, the notochord, and epidermis (Figure 2B, white arrow, white arrowhead, and gold arrow, respectively).
evidence: This is shown using an RA reporter line with immunohistochemistry.

claim: The epidermis is exposed to RA signaling.
source: The GFP expression indicates tissues that have been exposed to RA. These tissues included the adaxial region of the somites, the notochord, and epidermis (Figure 2B, white arrow, white arrowhead, and gold arrow, respectively).
evidence: This is shown using an RA reporter line with immunohistochemistry.

claim: Primitive angioblasts labeled with anti-Etv2 staining do not overlap with GFP staining from the RA reporter.
source: The primitive angioblasts, labeled with anti-Etv2 staining, do not overlap with GFP staining (Figure 2B, red arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry showing spatial separation of signals.

claim: Angioblasts are not receiving an RA signal.
source: Together, these results indicate that angioblasts are not receiving an RA signal and do not require RA signaling for migration when surrounded by a wild-type environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of overlap between RA reporter expression and angioblast markers.

claim: Angioblasts do not require RA signaling for migration when surrounded by a wild-type environment.
source: Together, these results indicate that angioblasts are not receiving an RA signal and do not require RA signaling for migration when surrounded by a wild-type environment.
evidence: This is demonstrated through transplantation experiments showing normal migration of RA-depleted cells in wild-type hosts.

claim: Wild-type cells transplanted into the notochord display normal angioblast migration to the midline.
source: Host embryos with wild-type cells transplanted to the notochord displayed normal angioblast migration to the midline (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown through transplantation experiments.

claim: tg(HS:dnRAR) cells transplanted into the notochord show normal midline angioblast migration.
source: Similarly, transplants of tg(HS:dnRAR) cells into the notochord showed normal midline angioblast migration (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown through transplantation experiments.

claim: In situ hybridizations against apela, aplnra, and aplnrb show little change in RA-depleted conditions.
source: In addition, in situ hybridizations against a known notochord-secreted angioblast chemoattractant apela, as well as the receptors aplnra and aplnrb, show little change in RA-depleted conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in situ hybridization experiments comparing control and RA-depleted conditions.

claim: The lack of RA signaling in notochord cells is not causing the angioblast migration defects.
source: This indicates that the lack of RA signaling in notochord cells is not causing the angioblast migration defects.
evidence: This is inferred from transplantation experiments and gene expression analysis.

claim: Wild-type cells transplanted into the somitic mesoderm show normal angioblast migration to the midline.
source: Wild-type cells transplanted into the somitic mesoderm showed normal angioblast migration to the midline (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is shown through transplantation experiments.

claim: tg(HS:dnRAR) cells transplanted into the somitic mesoderm cause angioblast migration defects in the region of the host embryo where they were transplanted.
source: However, when we transplanted tg(HS:dnRAR) cells into the somitic mesoderm, angioblasts showed migratory defects in the region of the host embryo in which they were transplanted (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through transplantation experiments showing regional defects.

claim: Fluorescence percentage at the midline in chimeric regions of the notochord shows no statistically significant difference compared to controls.
source: Quantification of fluorescence percentage at the midline, in the chimeric regions of the notochord, showed no statistically significant difference compared to controls (Figure 2I, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is quantified from fluorescence measurements in transplantation experiments.

claim: Fluorescence percentage in chimeric regions of the somites shows statistical significance between wild-type and tg(HS:dnRAR).
source: However, quantification of fluorescence percentage in the chimeric regions of the somites showed statistical significance between wild-type and tg(HS:dnRAR) (Figure 2J, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is quantified from fluorescence measurements in transplantation experiments.

claim: The somites are the principal tissue required for RA signaling-mediated midline angioblast migration.
source: This indicates that the somites are the principal tissue required for RA signaling-mediated midline angioblast migration.
evidence: This is concluded from transplantation experiments showing somite-specific effects.

claim: Noto is required for the formation of the notochord.
source: Noto is required for the formation of the notochord, and in the absence of Noto, the midline cells adopt a somitic fate (Talbot et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: In the absence of Noto, midline cells adopt a somitic fate.
source: Noto is required for the formation of the notochord, and in the absence of Noto, the midline cells adopt a somitic fate (Talbot et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous studies.

claim: In noto mutants, some angioblasts reach the midline at later developmental stages and resolve into a single blood vessel.
source: However, it is not clear if midline convergence was delayed or absent in notochord-less embryos. In noto mutants, some angioblasts reach the midline at later developmental stages and resolve into a single blood vessel (Fouquet et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from previous research.

claim: noto morphants show slowed angioblast migration.
source: Control morphant embryos show normal angioblast migration (Figure 3A), whereas noto morphants show slowed angioblast migration (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging of morphant embryos.

claim: Midline convergence occurs in both control and noto morphant embryos.
source: However, midline convergence still occurs in both conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown through quantification of embryos with midline angioblasts.

claim: The notochord is ultimately dispensable for the formation of the VMC and midline positioning of angioblasts.
source: This implies that the notochord is ultimately dispensable for the formation of the VMC and midline positioning of angioblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that angioblasts reach the midline in noto morphants.

claim: tbx16 is required for proper somite formation.
source: Previous studies have shown that the t-box transcription factor tbx16 is required for proper somite formation (Amacher et al., 2002; Goto et al., 2017; Griffin et al., 1998; Kimmel et al., 1989; Manning and Kimelman, 2015; Row et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: In the absence of Tbx16, cells that would normally join the paraxial mesoderm fail to do so, causing a deficiency in the trunk somitic mesoderm.
source: In the absence of Tbx16, cells that would normally join the paraxial mesoderm fail to do so, causing a deficiency in the trunk somitic mesoderm, but leaving the endothelium intact (Thompson et al., 1998).
evidence: This is cited from previous research.

claim: In tbx16-/- embryos, angioblast migration does not occur, and they remain in their positions in the lateral plate.
source: In wild-type sibling embryos, angioblast migration progresses normally to the midline (Figure 3D). However, in tbx16-/- embryos, angioblast migration does not occur, and they remain in their positions in the lateral plate (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging of tbx16 mutants.

claim: Angioblasts never reach the midline in any tbx16-/- embryo.
source: Fluorescence quantification indicated that angioblasts never reach the midline in any embryo (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is quantified from fluorescence measurements in tbx16 mutants.

claim: Embryos injected with noto morpholino have angioblasts located at the midline that appear to have resolved into one blood vessel structure.
source: Embryos injected with noto morpholino have angioblasts located at the midline that appear to have resolved into one blood vessel structure (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is shown through transverse sections of morphant embryos.

claim: Embryos injected with tbx16 morpholinos show two distinct vessels located on either side of the notochord.
source: Embryos injected with tbx16 morpholinos, however, show two distinct vessels located on either side of the notochord (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is shown through transverse sections of morphant embryos.

claim: The somites are critical for angioblast convergence at the midline.
source: This indicates that the somites are critical for angioblast convergence at the midline, while the notochord is ultimately dispensable.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing noto and tbx16 morphant phenotypes.

claim: The notochord is ultimately dispensable for angioblast convergence at the midline.
source: This indicates that the somites are critical for angioblast convergence at the midline, while the notochord is ultimately dispensable.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing noto and tbx16 morphant phenotypes.

claim: The relative location of the notochord in DMSO-treated embryos is in close proximity to the ventral underlying endoderm at the 12-somite stage.
source: The relative location of the notochord in DMSO-treated embryos was in close proximity to the ventral underlying endoderm at the 12-somite stage, but that distance increased by the 15-somite stage (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown through imaging of fixed embryos at different stages.

claim: The distance between the notochord and ventral underlying endoderm increases by the 15-somite stage in DMSO-treated embryos.
source: The relative location of the notochord in DMSO-treated embryos was in close proximity to the ventral underlying endoderm at the 12-somite stage, but that distance increased by the 15-somite stage (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown through imaging of fixed embryos at different stages.

claim: In DEAB-treated embryos, the notochord remains ventrally localized at both the 12-somite stage and 15-somite stage.
source: In DEAB-treated embryos, the notochord remains ventrally localized at both the 12-somite stage and 15-somite stage (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown through imaging of DEAB-treated fixed embryos.

claim: In RA-treated embryos, the notochord is prematurely dorsally localized at the 12-somite stage and extends even further by the 15-somite stage.
source: When the same experiment was done with embryos exposed to exogenous RA, the notochord was prematurely dorsally localized at the 12-somite stage and extended even further by the 15-somite stage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown through imaging of RA-treated fixed embryos.

claim: aldh1a2-/- embryos show delayed dorsal displacement relative to DMSO in both the timing of dorsal movement and the magnitude of that movement.
source: We found that aldh1a2-/- embryos showed delayed dorsal displacement relative to DMSO in both the timing of dorsal movement and the magnitude of that movement (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is quantified from time-lapse imaging measurements.

claim: As somites mature they extend in both the dorsal and ventral axis.
source: Previous work showed that as somites mature they extend in both the dorsal and ventral axis (Tlili et al., 2019), and based on this we hypothesized that this extension was concurrent with the dorsal translocation of the notochord.
evidence: This is cited from previous research and used to form a hypothesis.

claim: Somite extension is concurrent with the dorsal translocation of the notochord.
source: Previous work showed that as somites mature they extend in both the dorsal and ventral axis (Tlili et al., 2019), and based on this we hypothesized that this extension was concurrent with the dorsal translocation of the notochord.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous research and tested in the study.

claim: Trunk explants show notochord dorsal movement away from the autofluorescent yolk.
source: The notochord reporter showed clear dorsal movement away from the autofluorescent yolk (Figure 4H'–J').
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging of trunk explants.

claim: Somites show corresponding expansion along the dorsal-ventral axis during notochord dorsal movement.
source: The somites also showed the corresponding expansion along the dorsal-ventral axis (Figure 4H"–J").
evidence: This is demonstrated through time-lapse imaging of trunk explants.

claim: The proper development of the midline is both RA-dependent and requires only factors localized to the trunk of the embryo.
source: Together, this data indicates that the proper development of the midline is both RA-dependent and requires only factors localized to the trunk of the embryo.
evidence: This is concluded from trunk explant experiments showing autonomous midline development.

claim: As angioblasts approach the midline, a gap appears between notochord/hypochord and the underlying endoderm.
source: As angioblasts approach the midline, a gap appears between notochord/hypochord and the underlying endoderm (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning and imaging of embryos at different stages.

claim: The gap between notochord/hypochord and endoderm is acellular.
source: This gap is acellular as a 15 μm max projection shows an absence of both nuclei and F-actin labeling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through maximum projection imaging showing absence of cellular markers.

claim: The gap is filled by angioblasts by the 15-somite stage, separating the notochord from the endoderm.
source: This gap is filled by angioblasts by the 15-somite stage, separating the notochord from the endoderm (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning and imaging at the 15-somite stage.

claim: The process of dorsal translocation of the notochord is called notochord-endoderm separation (NES).
source: We call the process of dorsal translocation of the notochord the notochord-endoderm separation (NES).
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for the observed process.

claim: The transient opening that forms from NES is referred to as the ventral midline cavity (VMC).
source: The transient opening that forms from NES is referred to as the ventral midline cavity (VMC).
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors for the observed structure.

claim: Angioblast migration is largely complete for the fifth somite region of the trunk by the 18-somite stage.
source: As angioblast migration continues, additional angioblasts occupy the VMC until the 18-somite stage when angioblast migration is largely complete for the fifth somite region of the trunk (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning and imaging at the 18-somite stage.

claim: Embryos treated with exogenous RA and sectioned at the 12-somite stage show premature angioblast migration to the midline and NES.
source: Embryos sectioned at the 12-somite stage showed premature angioblast migration to the midline and NES, indicating that angioblast migration and NES are responsive to exogenous RA signal (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sectioning of RA-treated embryos.

claim: Angioblast migration and NES are responsive to exogenous RA signal.
source: Embryos sectioned at the 12-somite stage showed premature angioblast migration to the midline and NES, indicating that angioblast migration and NES are responsive to exogenous RA signal (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of premature migration and NES in RA-treated embryos.

claim: At the 12-somite stage in DEAB-treated embryos, the angioblasts are localized in the lateral plate mesoderm.
source: At the 12-somite stage, the angioblasts are localized in the lateral plate mesoderm (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning of DEAB-treated embryos.

claim: At the 12-somite stage in DEAB-treated embryos, the notochord remains flush against the endoderm with no visible VMC or NES.
source: Focusing on the midline of the embryo, we observe that the notochord remains flush against the endoderm with no visible VMC or NES (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning of DEAB-treated embryos at the 12-somite stage.

claim: At the 15-somite stage in DEAB-treated embryos, the notochord remains flush against the endoderm and no angioblasts have reached the midline.
source: At the 15-somite stage, we observe some midline movement of the angioblasts; however, the notochord remains flush against the endoderm and no angioblasts have been able to reach the midline (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning of DEAB-treated embryos at the 15-somite stage.

claim: At the 18-somite stage in DEAB-treated embryos, a small VMC has formed between the notochord and endoderm.
source: During the 18-somite stage, a small VMC has formed between the notochord and endoderm. The leading angioblasts have partially migrated into this VMC; however, the bulk of the angioblasts still reside outside of the midline (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning of DEAB-treated embryos at the 18-somite stage.

claim: By the 21-somite stage in DEAB-treated embryos, the angioblasts have largely resolved to the midline, although with some angioblasts still residing outside the midline.
source: By the 21-somite stage, the angioblasts have largely resolved to the midline, although with some angioblasts still residing outside the midline (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning of DEAB-treated embryos at the 21-somite stage.

claim: NES is a consequence of processive somite maturation that begins in the anterior regions and progresses posteriorly.
source: Given the pronounced delays in NES formation for anterior regions in RA-depleted embryos, we suspected that NES was a consequence of the known processive somite maturation that begins in the anterior regions and progresses posteriorly (Stern and Piatkowska, 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations and cited knowledge about somite maturation.

claim: In the more immature 12th somite, angioblasts reside in their lateral regions and NES is not pronounced.
source: In more immature 12th somite, angioblasts reside in their lateral regions and NES is not pronounced (white dashed lines outline the somites, and yellow brackets show the distance from the notochord to the ventral endoderm) (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning at different anterior-posterior positions.

claim: In the fifth somite of the same embryo, angioblasts reside at the midline and NES is very pronounced.
source: In the fifth somite of the same embryo, angioblasts reside at the midline and NES is very pronounced, indicating that NES occurs anterior to posteriorly (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning at different anterior-posterior positions.

claim: NES occurs anterior to posteriorly.
source: In the fifth somite of the same embryo, angioblasts reside at the midline and NES is very pronounced, indicating that NES occurs anterior to posteriorly (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing anterior and posterior somite regions in the same embryo.

claim: The angioblast migration percentage is not statistically significant between the 5th and 12th somite in RA-depletion conditions.
source: The angioblast migration percentage was not statistically significant between the 5th and 12th somite in RA-depletion conditions (p=0.33).
evidence: This is determined through statistical analysis of quantified data.

claim: The midline exists in a more immature state in RA-depleted conditions.
source: This indicates that the midline exists in a more immature state in RA-depleted conditions, and the more mature state provides space in which the angioblasts can migrate into.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing anterior and posterior regions in RA-depleted embryos.

claim: The more mature state of the midline provides space in which the angioblasts can migrate into.
source: This indicates that the midline exists in a more immature state in RA-depleted conditions, and the more mature state provides space in which the angioblasts can migrate into.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between somite maturation and angioblast migration.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of RA signaling causes a smaller than normal dorsal aorta.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of RA signaling has previously been shown to effect the zebrafish vasculature, notably causing a smaller than normal dorsal aorta (Pillay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous research.

claim: In aldh1a2-/- embryos, the size of the dorsal aorta is reduced but remained lumenized.
source: Images show that the dorsal aorta and posterior cardinal vein in wild-type embryos are roughly equivalent in size (Figure 6A, white arrows). However, in the aldh1a2-/- embryos, the size of the dorsal aorta is reduced but remained lumenized (Figure 6B, white arrows).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning and imaging of aldh1a2 mutants.

claim: The vasculature of aldh1a2-/- siblings shows a large reduction of the size of the dorsal aorta at 5 dpf.
source: However, the vasculature of the aldh1a2-/- siblings shows a large reduction of the size of the dorsal aorta (Figure 6D, white arrow).
evidence: This is shown through imaging of 5 dpf embryos.

claim: The posterior cardinal vein of aldh1a2-/- increased in size compared to its sibling.
source: In addition, it appears that the posterior cardinal vein of aldh1a2-/-increased in size compared to its sibling (Figure 6D, yellow arrowhead).
evidence: This is shown through imaging of 5 dpf embryos.

claim: DEAB-treated embryos show reduced cell number in the artery versus DMSO-treated embryos.
source: We see reduced cell number in the DEAB-treated artery versus the DMSO-treated artery (Figure 6E, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is quantified by counting nuclei in blood vessels.

claim: DEAB treatment corresponds to an increase in the number of cells in the veins compared to DMSO treatment.
source: This corresponds to an increase in the number of cells in the veins during DEAB treatment compared to DMSO.
evidence: This is quantified by counting nuclei in blood vessels.

claim: RA is required for the proper formation of the definitive vasculature.
source: While we cannot definitively say that the migration defects caused the arterial reduction, it indicates that RA is required for the proper formation of the definitive vasculature.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of vascular defects in RA-depleted conditions.

claim: Newly born somites initially lay flat and extend farther in the medial-lateral axis.
source: During normal development, newly born somites initially lay flat and extend farther in the medial-lateral axis, demonstrated by a section of 15-somite stage embryo at the 12th somite (Figure 7A, white dashed lines; Tlili et al., 2019).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning and cited from previous research.

claim: As somites mature, they narrow in the medial-lateral axis and extend in the dorsal-ventral axis.
source: However, as somites mature, they will narrow in the medial-lateral axis and extend in the dorsal-ventral axis, as demonstrated by a section of the fifth somite of a 15-somite stage embryo (Figure 7B, white dashed line; Tlili et al., 2019).
evidence: This is shown through sectioning and cited from previous research.

claim: Embryos transplanted with wild-type cells show little difference with the contralateral somite in terms of shape and maturation.
source: Embryos that were transplanted with wild-type cells showed little difference with the contralateral somite in terms of shape and maturation (Figure 7C, white dashed lines).
evidence: This is shown through transplantation experiments and imaging.

claim: Embryos transplanted with HS:dnRAR cells show a defect in the somite containing donor cells, with the somite extending farther in the medial-lateral axis while the contralateral somite extends farther in the dorsal-ventral axis.
source: However, embryos transplanted with HS:dnRAR cells showed a defect in the somite containing donor cells, with the somite extending farther in the medial-lateral axis while the contralateral somite extends farther in the dorsal-ventral axis (Figure 7D, white dashed lines).
evidence: This is shown through transplantation experiments and imaging.

claim: RA is required cell-autonomously for somite maturation and dorsal-ventral extension.
source: Together, this indicates that RA is required cell-autonomously for somite maturation and dorsal-ventral extension.
evidence: This is concluded from transplantation experiments showing cell-autonomous effects.

claim: Cells in DMSO-treated embryos show broad movements consistent with that of somite rotation.
source: Cells in the DMSO-treated embryos showed broad movements consistent with that of somite rotation, where cells located in the anterior of the somite will translocate to the posterior of the somite (Hollway et al., 2007; Figure 7F, white arrows).
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging of labeled cells and cited from previous research.

claim: Cells in DEAB-treated embryos show little intratissue displacement and cells largely remain static.
source: However, cells in the DEAB-treated embryos show little intratissue displacement and cells largely remained static (Figure 7G, white arrows).
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging of labeled cells in DEAB-treated embryos.

claim: Cells in DMSO-treated embryos show significant amounts of displacement throughout the somite.
source: Cells in the DMSO-treated embryos showed significant amounts of displacement throughout the somite ( Figure 7H, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is quantified from tracking cell movements in time-lapse imaging.

claim: DEAB-treated cells show less displacement over time compared to DMSO-treated cells.
source: However, the DEAB cells showed less displacement over time (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is quantified from tracking cell movements in time-lapse imaging.

claim: Quantification of speed shows no statistically significant difference between DMSO and DEAB treatment.
source: Quantification of speed in the same manner showed no statistically significant difference between DMSO and DEAB treatment (Figure 7I, Figure 7—source data 2).
evidence: This is quantified from tracking cell movements in time-lapse imaging.

claim: Cells in RA-depletion conditions show little directional movement compared to DMSO, indicating that cells are not moving in a manner consistent with reshaping of the somite.
source: A sample of somite cell tracks shows little directional movement in loss of RA conditions compared to DMSO, indicating that cells are not moving in a manner consistent with reshaping of the somite, as well as suggesting a role for RA signaling in somite rotation (Figure 7J and K, Videos 6 and 7, respectively).
evidence: This is shown through visualization of cell tracks in time-lapse imaging.

claim: RA signaling plays a role in somite rotation.
source: A sample of somite cell tracks shows little directional movement in loss of RA conditions compared to DMSO, indicating that cells are not moving in a manner consistent with reshaping of the somite, as well as suggesting a role for RA signaling in somite rotation (Figure 7J and K, Videos 6 and 7, respectively).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of reduced directional movement in RA-depleted conditions.

claim: The Cxcr4a/Cxcl12a signaling axis is responsible for controlling cell movements in the somite.
source: The Cxcr4a/Cxcl12a signaling axis has been shown to be responsible for controlling cell movements in the somite. In situ hybridization for cxcr4a shows a loss of expression in RA-depletion conditions and gain of expression in RA-addition conditions (Hollway et al., 2007; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is cited from previous research and confirmed through in situ hybridization.

claim: In situ hybridization for cxcr4a shows a loss of expression in RA-depletion conditions.
source: The Cxcr4a/Cxcl12a signaling axis has been shown to be responsible for controlling cell movements in the somite. In situ hybridization for cxcr4a shows a loss of expression in RA-depletion conditions and gain of expression in RA-addition conditions (Hollway et al., 2007; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is shown through in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: In situ hybridization for cxcr4a shows gain of expression in RA-addition conditions.
source: The Cxcr4a/Cxcl12a signaling axis has been shown to be responsible for controlling cell movements in the somite. In situ hybridization for cxcr4a shows a loss of expression in RA-depletion conditions and gain of expression in RA-addition conditions (Hollway et al., 2007; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is shown through in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: The ventral expansion of the somite that occurs during somite cell rearrangement and maturation is responsible for NES.
source: We speculated that the ventral expansion of the somite that occurs during somite cell rearrangement and maturation was responsible for NES.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested through measurements and analysis.

claim: A simple linear regression shows a slope of 0.002 and y-intercept of 1.04 for the relationship between ventral somite expansion and notochord-endoderm distance.
source: A simple linear regression of the data, indicated by the black line, shows a slope of 0.002 and y-intercept of 1.04 (Figure 7M, Figure 7—source data 3).
evidence: This is calculated from measurements over time.

claim: The flat slope indicates little variance across time in the relationship between ventral somite expansion and NES.
source: The flat slope indicates little variance across time, and the y-intercept near 1 indicates that NES is equivalent to ventral expansion of the somite.
evidence: This is interpreted from the linear regression analysis.

claim: NES is equivalent to ventral expansion of the somite.
source: The flat slope indicates little variance across time, and the y-intercept near 1 indicates that NES is equivalent to ventral expansion of the somite.
evidence: This is interpreted from the linear regression analysis showing a 1:1 correlation.

claim: The 1:1 correlation of ventral somite expansion and notochord displacement provides strong evidence that somite morphogenesis is critical for NES.
source: The 1:1 correlation of ventral somite expansion and notochord displacement, as well as the tbx16 loss-of-function NES defect, provides strong evidence that somite morphogenesis is critical for NES.
evidence: This is concluded from quantitative analysis and genetic experiments.

claim: At the 180' timepoint in live explants, angioblasts are not at the midline and the hypochord remains flush with the endoderm.
source: At the 180′ timepoint, angioblasts were not at the midline and the hypochord remained flush with the endoderm (Figure 7O, Video 8).
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging of live explants.

claim: By the 240' stage in live explants, the hypochord is separated away from the endoderm.
source: By the 240′ stage, the hypochord is separated away from the endoderm (Figure 7P), and shortly after this, the angioblasts are able to complete their migration to the midline by the 270′ timepoint (Figure 7P).
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging of live explants.

claim: Angioblasts complete their migration to the midline by the 270' timepoint in live explants.
source: By the 240′ stage, the hypochord is separated away from the endoderm (Figure 7P), and shortly after this, the angioblasts are able to complete their migration to the midline by the 270′ timepoint (Figure 7P).
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging of live explants.

claim: Live explants of embryos treated with DEAB show angioblast migration defects and lack of NES.
source: Similar to the results seen in fixed sections, live explants of embryos treated with DEAB show angioblast migration defects and lack of NES (Video 9).
evidence: This is shown through time-lapse imaging of DEAB-treated live explants.

claim: The emergence of the transient VMC is a necessary requirement for contralateral angioblasts to complete their migration and coalesce at the midline.
source: Here, we established a cell-nonautonomous angioblast migration model wherein shape changes in the somitic mesoderm create a physical space for angioblasts to migrate into and develop into the axial vasculature. The emergence of the transient VMC is a necessary requirement for contralateral angioblasts to complete their migration and coalesce at the midline.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: A defect in somitic mesoderm development in RA-depletion conditions delays somite maturation.
source: We observed a defect in somitic mesoderm development in RA-depletion conditions, which delayed somite maturation, intrasomite cellular movement, and significantly impeded NES.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple experiments.

claim: A defect in somitic mesoderm development in RA-depletion conditions delays intrasomite cellular movement.
source: We observed a defect in somitic mesoderm development in RA-depletion conditions, which delayed somite maturation, intrasomite cellular movement, and significantly impeded NES.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple experiments.

claim: A defect in somitic mesoderm development in RA-depletion conditions significantly impedes NES.
source: We observed a defect in somitic mesoderm development in RA-depletion conditions, which delayed somite maturation, intrasomite cellular movement, and significantly impeded NES.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple experiments.

claim: Addition of RA accelerates somite maturation and NES, along with angioblast migration.
source: Conversely, we found that addition of RA accelerated somite maturation and NES, along with angioblast migration.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from RA addition experiments.

claim: Loss of function of tbx16 prevents angioblast migration completely and results in bifurcated blood vessel formation.
source: Loss of function of tbx16 prevented angioblast migration completely and resulted in bifurcated blood vessel formation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from tbx16 mutant analysis.

claim: Changes in vascular morphology in tbx16 mutants indicate that the somitic mesoderm is a requirement for angioblast migration to the midline.
source: These changes in vascular morphology indicate that the somitic mesoderm is a requirement for angioblast migration to the midline.
evidence: This is concluded from the tbx16 mutant phenotype.

claim: In amniotes such as the mouse and quail, the dorsal aorta and cardinal vein are initially bifurcated in a similar manner to zebrafish tbx16 mutants prior to fusion at the midline.
source: It is notable that in amniotes, such as the mouse and quail, the dorsal aorta and cardinal vein are initially bifurcated in a similar manner to zebrafish tbx16 mutants prior to fusion at the midline (Drake and Fleming, 2000; Pardanaud et al., 1996; Pardanaud et al., 1987).
evidence: This is cited from previous research on amniote vascular development.

claim: Evolutionary differences in the somitic mesoderm between teleosts and amniotes could play a role in the differences in vascular development.
source: It is possible that evolutionary differences in the somitic mesoderm between teleosts and amniotes could play a role in the differences in vascular development.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparing zebrafish and amniote vascular development.

claim: The initiation of NES correlates very closely with angioblast migration.
source: Very little is known about the process of NES. Our observations indicate that its initiation correlates very closely with angioblast migration, with angioblasts migrating into the VMC seemingly as soon as it appears in both wild-type and RA-depletion conditions.
evidence: This is observed through time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: Angioblasts migrate into the VMC seemingly as soon as it appears in both wild-type and RA-depletion conditions.
source: Very little is known about the process of NES. Our observations indicate that its initiation correlates very closely with angioblast migration, with angioblasts migrating into the VMC seemingly as soon as it appears in both wild-type and RA-depletion conditions.
evidence: This is observed through time-lapse imaging experiments.

claim: Blood vessels need to achieve a sufficient volume for blood transport.
source: Given that these blood vessels become lumenized and need to achieve a sufficient volume for blood transport, it is plausible that they require morphological changes within the ventral part of the embryo to accommodate for their size.
evidence: This is general knowledge about blood vessel function.

claim: Blood vessels require morphological changes within the ventral part of the embryo to accommodate for their size.
source: Given that these blood vessels become lumenized and need to achieve a sufficient volume for blood transport, it is plausible that they require morphological changes within the ventral part of the embryo to accommodate for their size.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed correlation between VMC formation and angioblast migration.

claim: Delays in somite maturation prevent angioblasts from reaching the midline in a normal developmental time frame.
source: Delays in somite maturation prevent angioblasts from reaching the midline in a normal developmental time frame.
evidence: This is observed in RA-depletion experiments.

claim: The consequences of delayed angioblast migration may result in malformed blood vessel structure in RA-depleted embryos.
source: It is possible that the consequences of this migration defect result in the malformed blood vessel structure in RA-depleted embryos, which have small arteries and larger veins.
evidence: This is speculation connecting migration defects to vascular phenotypes.

claim: The most lateral angioblasts, which migrate later than more medial angioblasts, preferentially adopt a venous fate over an arterial one.
source: Prior work showed that the most lateral angioblasts, which migrate later than more medial angioblasts, preferentially adopt a venous fate over an arterial one (Kohli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous research.

claim: Somite maturation is a key factor in determining the proper distribution of endothelial progenitors to the arteries and veins by timing angioblast migration and altering cell fate decision patterns.
source: This implies that somite maturation is a key factor in determining the proper distribution of endothelial progenitors to the arteries and veins by essentially timing angioblast migration and altering cell fate decision patterns.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between migration timing and cell fate, combined with cited knowledge.

claim: The formation of the VMC does not necessarily require the notochord tissue itself.
source: We found that the formation of the VMC does not necessarily require the notochord tissue itself.
evidence: This is demonstrated through noto morphant experiments.

claim: In noto morphants, there is still a ventral cavity and angioblasts are able to arrive at the midline.
source: In noto morphants, which causes the notochord to adopt a somitic fate, there is still a ventral cavity and angioblasts are able to arrive at the midline.
evidence: This is demonstrated through noto morphant experiments.

claim: The migratory defects in noto mutants could be the result of reduced notochord-secreted factors such as apela.
source: The migratory defects could be the result of reduced notochord-secreted factors such as apela, which greatly reduce but do not completely abolish migration (Helker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on cited research about apela function.

claim: Signals from the notochord, such as Hedgehog, influence somite development, which in turn facilitates angioblast migration.
source: Another factor could be that signals from the notochord, such as Hedgehog, influence somite development, which in turn facilitates angioblast migration (Blagden et al., 1997; Hinits et al., 2009; Yin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation based on cited research about notochord signaling.

claim: Mechanical coupling between the somites and midline tissue is required such that somite morphogenesis drives the separation of the midline mesoderm away from the underlying endoderm.
source: While the fate of the midline tissue does not need to be notochord for NES to occur, it is likely that mechanical coupling between the somites and midline tissue is required such that somite morphogenesis drives the separation of the midline mesoderm away from the underlying endoderm.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in noto morphants where somitic tissue at the midline still allows NES.

claim: In noto loss of function, the somitic tissue that forms at the midline in place of notochord is continuous with the flanking somites.
source: In noto loss of function, the somitic tissue that forms at the midline in place of notochord is continuous with the flanking somites.
evidence: This is observed in noto morphant experiments.

claim: There is evidence of mechanical interactions of the somite and notochord during convergent extension, which are required for the remodeling of the adaxial cells.
source: In wild-type embryos, there is evidence of mechanical interactions of the somite and notochord during convergent extension, which are required for the remodeling of the adaxial cells, the medial most cells in the somite (Yin and Solnica-Krezel, 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous research.

claim: The phenotypes observed in both the somites and endothelium after loss of RA signaling are not the result of a simple deficit of mesoderm.
source: The phenotypes observed in both the somites and endothelium after loss of RA signaling are not the result of a simple deficit of mesoderm.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that somites still form but have maturation defects.

claim: RA signaling loss of function affects somite maturation and morphogenesis, but does not prevent somites from forming.
source: RA signaling loss of function affects somite maturation and morphogenesis, but does not prevent them from forming, and yet the migration of the angioblasts is still disrupted.
evidence: This is observed in RA-depletion experiments.

claim: The direct transcriptional targets of RA signaling that induce somite maturation are unknown.
source: The direct transcriptional targets of RA signaling that induce somite maturation are unknown, but it is clear that RA signaling controls the timing and progress of somite shape changes as they mature.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge while stating what is known.

claim: RA signaling controls the timing and progress of somite shape changes as they mature.
source: The direct transcriptional targets of RA signaling that induce somite maturation are unknown, but it is clear that RA signaling controls the timing and progress of somite shape changes as they mature.
evidence: This is demonstrated through RA manipulation experiments.

claim: Cell-autonomous effects of RA depletion on the somites, coupled with angioblast migration defects in RA-depleted somites, indicate that RA directly controls somite shape changes that facilitate migration.
source: Cell-autonomous effects of RA depletion on the somites, coupled with angioblast migration defects in RA-depleted somites, indicate that RA directly controls somite shape changes that facilitate migration.
evidence: This is concluded from transplantation experiments showing cell-autonomous effects.

claim: Somites can adopt mature shapes in explants, even in the absence of adjacent somites.
source: The fact that somites can adopt mature shapes in explants, even in the absence of adjacent somites, indicates this control is local to individual somites.
evidence: This is demonstrated through trunk explant experiments.

claim: RA signaling control of somite maturation is local to individual somites.
source: The fact that somites can adopt mature shapes in explants, even in the absence of adjacent somites, indicates this control is local to individual somites.
evidence: This is inferred from trunk explant experiments showing autonomous maturation.

claim: Loss of RA signaling activity in a relatively few number of adaxially localized cells in chimeric somites is sufficient to cause somite shape and angioblast migration defects.
source: It is also noteworthy that loss of RA signaling activity in a relatively few number of adaxially localized cells in our chimeric somites was sufficient to cause somite shape and angioblast migration defects.
evidence: This is observed in chimeric transplantation experiments.

claim: The somite cells most medial to the midline could be the population required for the ventral expansion of the somite and NES.
source: This implies that the somite cells most medial to the midline could be the population required for the ventral expansion of the somite and NES.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that adaxial cells are sufficient to cause defects.

claim: Some midline-directed cellular movement occurs in DEAB-treated embryos before NES is visibly seen.
source: It is not clear if NES is required for the initiation of angioblast migration as some midline-directed cellular movement occurs in DEAB-treated embryos before NES is visibly seen.
evidence: This is observed in time-lapse imaging of DEAB-treated embryos.

claim: The somite itself could facilitate the angioblasts' movement to the midline or simply provide an opening through which angioblasts can reach the midline.
source: It is possible that the somite itself could facilitate the angioblasts' movement to the midline or simply provide an opening through which angioblasts can reach the midline.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of somite influence on angioblast migration.

claim: Angioblasts are not sufficient to drive NES or their coalescence at the midline.
source: The fact that angioblasts reside adjacent to the notochord in tbx16 mutants, but do not migrate beneath them, implies that angioblasts are not sufficient to drive NES or their coalescence at the midline.
evidence: This is inferred from the tbx16 mutant phenotype.

claim: Ventral expansions of the somite drive the notochord away from the endoderm.
source: It is likely that ventral expansions of the somite drive the notochord away from the endoderm.
evidence: This is inferred from the 1:1 correlation between somite expansion and notochord displacement.

claim: Somitic maturation requires tight spatial and temporal control to facilitate the concomitant development of the endothelium.
source: Together, this indicates that somitic maturation requires tight spatial and temporal control to facilitate the concomitant development of the endothelium.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on all the findings of the study.
